triage.name: Marasmus
triage.reason: Severe wasting from inadequate energy intake; diagnosis is clinical from growth and dietary history with a recognizable exam.

demographics: Most common in infants and young children in settings of poverty, famine, or food insecurity
Occurs worldwide, including in the US in cases of neglect, food insecurity, or chronic illness
In adults, seen with severe self-neglect, eating disorders, or chronic disease

risk_factors.text: Neglect or caregiver inability to feed
Early weaning or improper formula preparation

chief_complaints.text: My child is very thin and not growing
He/she is irritable and cries a lot

hpi.progression: Progressive weight loss and wasting; child becomes increasingly irritable and hungry, then lethargic

atypical.how_it_differs: Presents with generalized weakness, weight loss, and functional decline; often mistaken for normal aging or frailty.
In children, marasmus often presents with failure to thrive, developmental delay, and recurrent infections; may be mistaken for other causes of failure to thrive.

general.mild: Thin, alert, irritable but consolable; appears younger than stated age
general.moderate: Markedly wasted with prominent ribs and limbs, irritable and demanding, sparse hair
general.severe: Severe generalized wasting, old-looking facies, apathetic or irritable, weak cry, no edema
general.critical: Cachectic and lethargic, hypotensive, hypothermic, too weak to feed, appears moribund

findings.maneuver: Inspect and palpate the limbs, buttocks, and temporal regions
findings.finding: Generalized loss of muscle bulk with prominent ribs and wasted buttocks

findings.maneuver: Pinch the skin over the abdomen, thigh, and upper arm
findings.finding: Loss of subcutaneous fat with loose, easily lifted skin folds

findings.maneuver: Weigh the child and plot weight for age on a growth chart
findings.finding: Weight far below the expected range for age, with weight-for-height preserved relative to height

findings.maneuver: Measure length or height and plot on a growth chart
findings.finding: Length or height below the expected range for age

findings.maneuver: Measure occipitofrontal circumference and plot on a growth chart
findings.finding: Head circumference below the expected range for age

findings.maneuver: Inspect the face and compare with expected appearance for age
findings.finding: Wizened, aged facial appearance with prominent cheekbones and sunken cheeks
Sunken eyes with loss of periorbital fat
Sparse, dry, brittle hair that pulls out easily

findings.maneuver: Inspect the lips and oral commissures
findings.finding: Fissuring and erythema at the corners of the mouth
Dry, scaly, inelastic skin with reduced turgor

findings.maneuver: Pinch and lift the abdominal skin
findings.finding: Loose abdominal skin folds with little underlying fat

findings.maneuver: Press the dorsum of the feet and the pretibial area for several seconds
findings.finding: No pitting edema

findings.maneuver: Palpate the right upper quadrant below the costal margin
findings.finding: Liver edge not palpable below the costal margin
Mild abdominal distension with tympany
Irritable, crying, and difficult to console, but alert and responsive

findings.maneuver: Observe the level of alertness and response to stimulation
findings.finding: Lethargic, drowsy, and slow to respond
Milestones not met for age

findings.maneuver: Test proximal strength by asking the child to sit up or lift the arms
findings.finding: Weakness with poor head control or inability to sit unsupported

findings.maneuver: Inspect the skin of the legs, buttocks, and perineum
findings.finding: No hyperpigmented, desquamating plaques with peeling edges

labs.caveat: Albumin is usually normal or only mildly low in marasmus; marked hypoalbuminemia with edema suggests kwashiorkor instead.
Anemia is common from iron, folate, or protein deficiency and from concurrent infection or parasites.
Microcytosis suggests iron deficiency; macrocytosis suggests folate or B12 deficiency.
Relative lymphocytosis can reflect concurrent viral or other infection.
Hyponatremia from poor intake, diarrhea, or refeeding; correct slowly.
Hypokalemia from diarrhea and poor intake; watch during refeeding.
Low bicarbonate suggests metabolic acidosis from diarrhea or starvation ketosis.
Elevated from dehydration and poor intake.
Creatinine may look near normal despite poor renal function because of very low muscle mass.
Hypoglycemia is a common and dangerous complication, especially in young children.
Hypophosphatemia is common and can worsen with refeeding; monitor closely.
Low total calcium often reflects low albumin; check ionized calcium if symptomatic.
Starvation ketosis from prolonged inadequate energy intake.
Check to exclude hypothyroidism as a cause of poor growth; results may be altered by illness.
Consider only if adrenal insufficiency is suspected.

findings.finding: Sinus tachycardia
Prolonged QT interval from hypocalcemia or hypokalemia
ST depression or flattened T waves with hypokalemia
Sinus bradycardia in severe hypothermia or terminal state

Hilar adenopathy or apical infiltrate suggesting tuberculosis

confirmatory.why: Confirms inadequate energy intake and quantifies degree of wasting; diagnosis of marasmus is clinical from growth and dietary history

Iron stores; may be elevated by inflammation
Deficiency can cause anemia and neurologic findings
Screens for chronic infection or inflammation
Chronic infection increases metabolic demand and causes wasting
supporting.only_if: risk factors or recurrent infections are present
respiratory symptoms, fever, or suspected tuberculosis

Bone age radiograph of the left hand and wrist
supporting.why: Documents delayed skeletal maturation from chronic undernutrition

Not routine; order only when respiratory infection or tuberculosis is suspected

not_indicated.why: Not routine; order only for suspected malabsorption or anatomic cause

not_indicated.test: Bone age radiograph of the left hand and wrist
not_indicated.why: Not routine; order only when growth failure is prominent

decision_points: Check glucose immediately in any lethargic or seizing child
Correct electrolytes and phosphate before and during refeeding to prevent refeeding syndrome
Distinguish marasmus (no edema) from kwashiorkor (edema, hypoalbuminemia, hepatomegaly)
Screen for and treat concurrent infection, which is often subtle and may be the presenting problem

criteria.name: WHO severe acute malnutrition (wasting) criteria
criteria.summary: Severe wasting is defined by a weight-for-height z-score below -3, mid-upper arm circumference below 115 mm in children 6-59 months, or bilateral pitting edema; marasmus is the non-edematous form.

differential.name: Kwashiorkor
differential.why_considered: Both are forms of severe protein-energy malnutrition with growth failure and wasting in young children.
differential.trigger: Bilateral pitting edema, especially in a child with a swollen abdomen and peeling skin

history: Diet often protein-poor but energy-adequate (e.g., starchy gruel)
Child may be apathetic and anorexic rather than hungry
Often after abrupt weaning or a diarrheal illness
exam: Bilateral pitting edema of feet and legs
Moon facies and a distended abdomen
Flaky paint dermatosis with hyperpigmented peeling plaques
Hepatomegaly from fatty liver
labs: Edema despite preserved or increased body weight
imaging: Ultrasound may show an enlarged, echogenic fatty liver

differential.name: Failure to thrive from non-organic causes
differential.why_considered: Poor weight gain and a thin child are the shared presenting problem, and psychosocial causes are common.

history: Feeding difficulties or caregiver-child interaction problems rather than absolute food scarcity
Weight may cross percentiles downward but height and head circumference are often preserved
No history of famine, poverty, or prolonged inadequate intake
exam: Mild to moderate underweight without the severe generalized muscle wasting and loss of subcutaneous fat of marasmus
No old-looking facies or sparse hair
Normal or near-normal developmental milestones
labs: Usually normal albumin, electrolytes, and glucose

differential.name: Celiac disease
differential.why_considered: Malabsorption causes weight loss, diarrhea, and failure to grow in children.

history: Chronic diarrhea, bloating, and foul-smelling stools
Symptoms worsen with gluten-containing foods
Family history of celiac disease or autoimmune disease
exam: Abdominal distension with wasted extremities
May have dermatitis herpetiformis
Growth failure with preserved or only mildly reduced subcutaneous fat early on
labs: Positive tissue transglutaminase IgA and endomysial antibodies
Iron deficiency anemia and low folate
Small bowel biopsy showing villous atrophy

differential.name: Cystic fibrosis
differential.why_considered: Pancreatic insufficiency and chronic lung disease cause poor weight gain and wasting in children.

history: Recurrent respiratory infections and chronic cough
Bulky, greasy, foul-smelling stools (steatorrhea)
Meconium ileus or family history of cystic fibrosis
exam: Digital clubbing and chronic lung findings
Nasal polyps
Salt-tasting skin
labs: Elevated sweat chloride on sweat testing
Pancreatic insufficiency with low fecal elastase
imaging: Chest x-ray with hyperinflation, bronchiectasis, or mucus plugging

differential.name: Chronic infection (tuberculosis or HIV)
differential.why_considered: Chronic infection increases metabolic demand and causes wasting, weight loss, and failure to thrive.
differential.trigger: Fever, night sweats, chronic cough, or known exposure to tuberculosis or HIV

history: Fever, night sweats, and chronic cough
Known contact with tuberculosis or risk factors for HIV
Weight loss despite adequate food intake
exam: Lymphadenopathy
Respiratory findings such as crackles or dullness
Oral thrush or other opportunistic findings if HIV
labs: Positive tuberculin skin test or interferon-gamma release assay
imaging: Chest x-ray with hilar adenopathy, apical infiltrate, or miliary pattern

differential.name: Hypothyroidism
differential.why_considered: Causes poor growth, weight gain or failure to thrive, and developmental delay in children.

history: Constipation, cold intolerance, and excessive sleepiness
Developmental delay and poor school performance
Family history of thyroid disease
exam: Coarse facial features, macroglossia, and dry skin
Bradycardia and delayed relaxation of deep tendon reflexes
Umbilical hernia
labs: Elevated TSH with low free T4
imaging: Thyroid ultrasound may show a small or absent gland

differential.name: Adrenal insufficiency
differential.why_considered: Can cause weight loss, weakness, and poor growth in children.

history: Fatigue, weakness, and salt craving
Nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain
History of steroid use or autoimmune disease
exam: Hyperpigmentation of skin creases and mucosa
Hypotension and tachycardia
Weight loss without the severe muscle wasting of marasmus
labs: Low morning cortisol with elevated ACTH

severity.mild: Early inadequate energy intake: weight faltering on the growth chart, mild loss of subcutaneous fat, alert and active child, no edema, normal electrolytes and glucose.
severity.moderate: Established marasmus: marked weight loss and muscle wasting, prominent ribs and wasted buttocks, irritability and constant hunger, sparse hair, dry skin, mild electrolyte abnormalities.
severity.severe: Severe wasting: weight-for-height z-score below -3 or mid-upper arm circumference below 115 mm, old-looking facies, apathy or lethargy, weak cry, hypoglycemia, hypokalemia, and hypophosphatemia.
severity.critical: Marasmic shock or severe dehydration: lethargic or unresponsive, hypotensive, hypothermic, too weak to feed, severe hypoglycemia and electrolyte derangements, high risk of death without immediate resuscitation.

red_flags.meaning: Severe hypoglycemia, dehydration, or sepsis; check glucose immediately and resuscitate
Life-threatening in young children; treat immediately with oral or intravenous glucose
Severe malnutrition with impaired thermoregulation; sign of critical illness

red_flags.finding: Hypotension or tachycardia out of proportion
red_flags.meaning: Shock from dehydration, sepsis, or heart failure; needs urgent fluids and evaluation

red_flags.finding: Severe dehydration or sunken eyes with no tears
red_flags.meaning: Diarrheal dehydration is a leading cause of death in severe malnutrition
Suggests kwashiorkor or a mixed picture rather than pure marasmus; changes management

red_flags.finding: Fever or hypothermia with no obvious source
red_flags.meaning: Concurrent infection is common and often subtle; sepsis must be excluded

complications.name: Hypoglycemia
clues: Worse after long periods without feeding

complications.name: Dehydration and electrolyte imbalance
clues: Sunken eyes and reduced skin turgor

complications.name: Refeeding syndrome
clues: Hypophosphatemia, hypokalemia, and hypomagnesemia after starting feeds

complications.name: Growth failure and developmental delay
clues: Height and head circumference below expected for age

complications.name: Anemia
clues: Microcytosis from iron deficiency or macrocytosis from folate or B12 deficiency

special_populations.differences: Marasmus most often presents in infants under 1 year; hypoglycemia and hypothermia are more frequent and more dangerous, and feeding must be advanced very cautiously to avoid refeeding syndrome.
Growth failure, developmental delay, and recurrent infections are prominent; weight-for-height and mid-upper arm circumference are used to grade severity, and catch-up growth may take months.
Presents with generalized weakness, weight loss, and functional decline; often mistaken for normal aging or frailty, and concurrent chronic disease and polypharmacy are common.

Maternal marasmus increases the risk of low birth weight, preterm birth, and intrauterine growth restriction; nutritional rehabilitation must meet the increased energy and protein demands of pregnancy.
Concurrent infection is more likely and may be the presenting problem; fever may be blunted, and a lower threshold for sepsis workup is needed.

key_questions.question: What has the child been eating and how often? Has there been enough food in the home?
key_questions.looking_for: Prolonged inadequate energy intake; food insecurity, famine, or neglect

key_questions.question: How has the child's weight changed over the past weeks to months?
key_questions.looking_for: Progressive weight loss and failure to gain weight over months

key_questions.question: Is the child always hungry and demanding food?
key_questions.looking_for: Constant hunger and irritability, which favor marasmus over kwashiorkor

key_questions.question: Has the child had swelling of the feet, legs, or face?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent edema; bilateral pitting edema suggests kwashiorkor or a mixed picture

key_questions.question: How has the child's behavior and activity level been?
key_questions.looking_for: Irritable and alert early; lethargy and apathy suggest severe disease

key_questions.question: Any diarrhea, vomiting, or poor feeding?
key_questions.looking_for: Diarrhea and vomiting causing dehydration and electrolyte losses

key_questions.question: Any fever, cough, or recurrent infections?
key_questions.looking_for: Concurrent infection, which is common and often subtle

key_questions.question: Was the child breastfed, and when and how was weaning done? How is formula prepared?
key_questions.looking_for: Early weaning or improperly prepared formula leading to inadequate intake

key_questions.question: Does the child have any chronic illness such as heart disease, cystic fibrosis, celiac disease, or kidney disease?
key_questions.looking_for: Chronic disease increasing metabolic demand or causing malabsorption

key_questions.question: Is the child on any medications or supplements?
key_questions.looking_for: Medications that suppress appetite or cause nutrient loss

key_questions.question: Who prepares and offers the child's meals, and what is the home situation?
key_questions.looking_for: Poverty, food insecurity, neglect, or caregiver inability to feed

key_questions.question: Has the child been exposed to tuberculosis or is there any known HIV risk in the household?
key_questions.looking_for: Chronic infection as a cause of wasting

key_questions.question: Is the child too weak to feed, drowsy, or difficult to wake?
key_questions.looking_for: Lethargy or unresponsiveness suggesting hypoglycemia, dehydration, or sepsis

reasoning_points: Gradual, progressive weight loss and failure to thrive over weeks to months from prolonged inadequate energy intake
Generalized muscle wasting and loss of subcutaneous fat with prominent ribs and wasted buttocks
Constant hunger and irritability rather than anorexia and apathy
No edema, no hepatomegaly, and no flaky paint dermatosis, distinguishing marasmus from kwashiorkor
Weight far below expected for age with relative preservation of weight-for-height early on
Risk factors such as poverty, food insecurity, neglect, early weaning, or chronic illness
Complications considered: hypoglycemia, dehydration and electrolyte losses, concurrent infection, and refeeding syndrome

easy: Infant or young child with months of inadequate food intake and severe visible wasting
Prominent ribs, wasted buttocks, and loose skin folds with no edema
Weight far below expected for age on the growth chart
medium: Child with failure to thrive where the dietary history is initially vague
Mild to moderate wasting without the classic old-looking facies
Concurrent diarrhea causing dehydration and electrolyte abnormalities
Distinguishing marasmus from kwashiorkor when some edema is present
hard: Older adult with self-neglect or an eating disorder presenting with weakness and weight loss mistaken for frailty
Child with an underlying chronic illness such as cystic fibrosis or celiac disease causing the wasting
Lethargic child with hypoglycemia where the malnutrition is not immediately recognized
Mixed marasmus-kwashiorkor picture with edema and hypoalbuminemia
Concurrent tuberculosis or HIV presenting primarily with wasting
